name: The One Gene-One Enzyme Hypothesis
statement: Each gene works by directing the making of one specific enzyme.
meaning: The one gene-one enzyme hypothesis is the proposition that genes act by controlling the production of specific enzymes, with each gene responsible for a single enzyme that in turn governs a single step in a metabolic pathway. It gave the abstract Mendelian gene a concrete job: to specify a particular protein. In its original form it drew a clean one-to-one line from gene to enzyme to biochemical reaction, a picture later refined but historically transformative.
mechanism: Beadle and Tatum irradiated the bread mould Neurospora to create mutants, then grew them on minimal medium. Mutants that could no longer synthesise a specific nutrient needed it supplied, and each such defect traced to a mutation in a single gene blocking a single metabolic step. This linked one gene to one enzyme to one reaction, showing that genes exert their effects through the enzymes they specify. The idea built on Garrod's earlier notion of inborn errors of metabolism, in which a heritable defect disrupts a specific biochemical step.

examples.text: X-rayed bread-mould strains that lost the ability to make a particular vitamin or amino acid each carried a single-gene defect blocking one biosynthetic step, the founding evidence.
Archibald Garrod's study of alkaptonuria as a heritable metabolic defect, an early precursor linking a gene to a specific biochemical step.
Hemoglobin, built from chains encoded by different genes, showed the unit is better stated as the polypeptide than the whole enzyme, a first refinement.

variants.name: One gene-one polypeptide
variants.text: The refinement recognising that many proteins are built from several polypeptide chains encoded by different genes, so the gene specifies a chain rather than a whole enzyme.

variants.name: The modern complications
variants.text: Alternative splicing, genes encoding functional RNA rather than protein, polycistronic messages, and post-translational modification, which break even the one-gene-one-polypeptide picture.

whyItMatters: It forged the first concrete, experimentally grounded link between genes and metabolism, turning the abstract gene into something that acts through specific proteins. This became a foundation of molecular biology and biochemical genetics, helped drive the search for the chemical nature of the gene, and earned Beadle and Tatum a share of the 1958 Nobel Prize, marking a pivotal step from classical genetics toward the molecular understanding of heredity.

working.text: read a gene's action as specifying a protein that carries out a biochemical function, the hypothesis's core insight.
map a heritable metabolic defect to a single gene blocking a single reaction, as Beadle and Tatum did.
treat the clean gene-to-enzyme mapping as a historically pivotal first approximation, since modern genetics is more complex.

limits: The strong form proved too simple and was progressively revised. Many proteins are built from several polypeptide chains encoded by different genes, so the unit became one gene-one polypeptide, and even that is incomplete because of alternative splicing, which lets one gene yield many proteins, genes that encode functional RNA rather than protein, polycistronic messages carrying several proteins, overlapping genes, and post-translational modification. It remains historically foundational but superseded in its literal one-to-one form.
misreadings: It is not still literally true that every gene maps to exactly one enzyme; alternative splicing, multi-subunit proteins, and RNA-only genes all break the one-to-one mapping. It does not mean all genes encode enzymes, since many encode structural or regulatory proteins or functional RNAs. Beadle and Tatum did not coin the catchy name, which came later; their own paper was more cautiously worded. And the 1958 Nobel citation honoured genes regulating chemical events, with a third laureate recognised for separate work.
origin: Proposed by George Beadle and Edward Tatum from their 1941 experiments on Neurospora, building on Archibald Garrod's earlier concept of inborn errors of metabolism, and honoured with a share of the 1958 Nobel Prize.

sources.text: Beadle & Tatum, "Genetic Control of Biochemical Reactions in Neurospora," PNAS 27 (1941): 499-506. — the founding experiments.
One gene-one enzyme hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the hypothesis, its Garrod precursor, and its progressive refinement.
